explanations.answer: The branches of the forest trees
explanations.explanation: That's the one, friend. God asks, "…how does the wood of the vine surpass any other branch among the trees in the forest?" (Ezekiel 15:2) It's a setup question, and the answer He's heading toward is that it doesn't. Vine wood is standing in a lineup of tall trees with nothing to brag about.

explanations.answer: The reeds of the Nile river
explanations.explanation: Reeds are a fun guess, but the Nile isn't in this question. God compares the vine's wood to "…any other branch among the trees in the forest?" (Ezekiel 15:2) So the lineup is branches from forest trees. Nobody is wading into a river here, and I'm glad, because I'd keep my base dry.

explanations.answer: The stalks of the wheat field
explanations.explanation: Wheat is a lovely guess, friend, but you wandered right out of the woods. God asks how the wood of the vine compares to "…any other branch among the trees in the forest?" (Ezekiel 15:2) Vine wood is up against forest branches, and honestly, I'd be nervous standing in that lineup too.

explanations.answer: A peg to hang utensils on
explanations.explanation: Yes! God asks, "Or can one make from it a peg on which to hang utensils?" (Ezekiel 15:3) That's about the smallest job you can give a piece of wood. It's just a little hook on the wall. And God is asking whether vine wood can even do that.

An ax handle is a solid guess, but it isn't what God asks about. He asks about "…a peg on which to hang utensils?" (Ezekiel 15:3) That's a tiny job, just a little hook on the wall. The question is whether vine wood could manage even that.

A shepherd's rod is a good guess, but it isn't in this verse. God asks whether one can make from vine wood "…a peg on which to hang utensils?" (Ezekiel 15:3) A peg is about as small and ordinary as a job gets. That's the point of asking.

Fire it is. God says, "No, it is cast into the fire for fuel." (Ezekiel 15:4) He asks what the wood could become, and the answer is that it gets burned. Nothing gets built from it. It just goes into the flames.

The sea is a big, dramatic guess, friend, but nobody's getting soaked in this verse. God says, "No, it is cast into the fire for fuel." (Ezekiel 15:4) The vine wood heads toward the flames, not the waves. It stays dry as a cookie left out overnight.

A pit sounds gloomy enough, but it's not the word here. God says the vine wood "…is cast into the fire for fuel." (Ezekiel 15:4) Then He adds, "The fire devours both ends, and the middle is charred." The pit will have to wait for another verse.

True. God says, "Even when it was whole, it could not be made useful." (Ezekiel 15:5) So the fire isn't the reason the wood is no good for building. Whole, it still couldn't make anything useful. Then He adds how much less it can be useful once the fire has charred it.

This one's actually true. God says, "Even when it was whole, it could not be made useful." (Ezekiel 15:5) That's before any fire touched it. Then He goes further: "How much less can it ever be useful when the fire has consumed it and charred it!" It's an easy one to second-guess, so don't beat yourself up.

Jerusalem is right. God says, "Like the wood of the vine among the trees of the forest, which I have given to the fire for fuel, so I will give up the people of Jerusalem." (Ezekiel 15:6) All those questions about wood were building to this. The vine in the picture stands for the people of Jerusalem.

Nineveh is a fine guess, friend, but it isn't in this verse. God says, "…so I will give up the people of Jerusalem." (Ezekiel 15:6) He is speaking about Jerusalem here. The vine wood given to the fire is the picture He uses for them.

Egypt turns up a lot in Scripture, but it isn't in this verse. God says, "…so I will give up the people of Jerusalem." (Ezekiel 15:6) That's where all the vine talk lands. The people of Jerusalem are the ones in the picture.

Not quite, friend. God says, "Though they may have escaped the fire, yet another fire will consume them." (Ezekiel 15:7) Getting out of one fire doesn't mean they're done with fire. It's a heavy line, and the text doesn't soften it.

False is right. God says, "Though they may have escaped the fire, yet another fire will consume them." (Ezekiel 15:7) Escaping once doesn't mean they're safe from then on. The text says another fire is coming for them.
That's it. God says, "…when I set My face against them, you will know that I am the LORD." (Ezekiel 15:7) What gets known is who He is. That is the point of the verse.

That's the opposite of where this verse goes, friend. God says, "…when I set My face against them, you will know that I am the LORD." (Ezekiel 15:7) What gets known is who He is. The city standing isn't part of it, and the verse before this one says He will give up the people of Jerusalem.

explanations.answer: That the vine will grow back
explanations.explanation: A comeback story would be nice, but this verse doesn't give one. God says, "…when I set My face against them, you will know that I am the LORD." (Ezekiel 15:7) What gets known is who He is. Nothing here says the vine grows back.

Yes. God says, "Thus I will make the land desolate, because they have acted unfaithfully…" (Ezekiel 15:8) The text gives the reason right there. It's a heavy one, and I think it's the part of this passage that hurts most.

explanations.answer: The people have lost too many battles
explanations.explanation: Battles aren't what this verse names. God says, "Thus I will make the land desolate, because they have acted unfaithfully…" (Ezekiel 15:8) The reason He gives is that they acted unfaithfully. I think that's a heavy thing to hear, so go gently with it.

explanations.answer: The people have stopped tending the vines
explanations.explanation: I see why the vine talk makes that tempting. But God gives a different reason: "Thus I will make the land desolate, because they have acted unfaithfully…" (Ezekiel 15:8) The vine is a picture of the people, not a farm chore they skipped. The reason is that they acted unfaithfully.
